activity: to build a model of an atom with protons, neutrons and electrons in the right places
knowledge_domain: to build a model of an atom with protons, neutrons and electrons in the right places
fact: An element's atomic number is the number of protons in the nucleus of each of its atoms; every carbon atom, for example, has exactly 6 protons.
story:
Florence dumped a shoebox of supplies onto the kitchen table: translucent blue beads, gray clay, a tangle of craft wire, and a printout of the periodic table she'd been allowed to take home from Mr. Chea's class. Each student had to participate by building a model of an atom, and hers was due Friday. There was only one problem, and it was a big one. She had no idea how many of anything to use.

Her friend Samantha had wanted the coolest element in the room, which was why Samantha had chosen gold and was already painting ping-pong balls shiny. "What did you get?" Samantha asked, appearing at the door with her backpack still on. Florence slid the periodic table across the table and pointed at the box marked C. "Carbon. But look, there's this little 6 on it, and I don't know what it's counting. Six what? Beads? Electrons? Grams of clay?"

Samantha squinted at the paper. "My gold has a 79. If it's counting something, that's a lot of something." They tried a theory: maybe the number counted electrons, since electrons were the small ones that spun around the outside. Florence strung six blue beads onto a wire ring and held it up. Then she frowned. "But if it's electrons, how do I know how many protons go in the middle? There has to be a rule, or nobody could build any of these." She turned the printout over and found a note in Mr. Chea's handwriting at the bottom. It read: "Dear builders. That number is the atomic number. It is the number of protons in the nucleus of each of its atoms. Every carbon atom, for example, has exactly 6 protons. Build carefully, and don't eat the clay. Mr. Chea."

Florence read it twice, then laughed so hard she had to sit down. "It's protons! Six protons, right in the middle!" She pinched off six balls of gray clay and squashed them together with some extra blobs for neutrons, then rehung her six electrons on the wire ring. Samantha held up her gold model, which now had seventy-nine clay balls crammed into a nucleus the size of an orange. "This," Samantha said, "is the heaviest fruit ever."

Florence balanced her carbon atom on a fork so the electrons could spin, and gave it one slow twist to watch it go.

activity: getting a first phone and learning to use it responsibly
knowledge_domain: getting a first phone and learning to use it responsibly
fact: Two-factor authentication asks for a second proof, such as a code sent to your phone, so a stolen password alone is not enough to get into an account.
story:
The sign in the window said the trade-in deal ended at six o'clock sharp, and it was already ten past five. Grace stood at the counter while Mr. Vu slid a slim black phone across the glass, the same model her cousin had, though her cousin's had a case made of that synthetic leather that peeled after a month. She picked this one up anyway, holding it like something that might go off.

"First phone," said Mr. Vu, watching her face. "Big deal."

"Big responsibility," Grace said, mostly because of last summer. She could still remember sitting on Dalia's back steps, spelling out her password out loud, letter by letter, so Dalia could log in on the library laptop. Dalia had winced even then and said, "You sure?" and Grace had said of course she was sure, it was faster than typing it herself. Now, waiting for Mr. Vu to set up the family plan, she wondered how many other people had been standing in that yard hearing every letter.

Dalia was there too, leaning on the counter beside her, when Dalia's own phone buzzed. She frowned at it. "Weird. I got a code." She turned the screen so Grace could see a text with six digits. "I didn't ask for a code. I'm not logging into anything."

Grace's stomach dropped, and the reasoning lined up fast and cold. The code had to come from somewhere. Codes arrive when somebody tries to get into an account, and that somebody had to know the password first, otherwise the account would never have moved far enough to send anything. "Dalia. Somebody has your password. That's why the code came. It's the second proof, like a lock after the lock, so a stolen password alone isn't enough to get in. Somebody's trying, and failing, right now."

"Two-factor authentication," Dalia said slowly, reading the words off the message. "I turned that on after you told me to. Remember? Last fall."

Grace did remember, and the memory cut both ways. She changed Dalia's password right there at the counter, fast, while Mr. Vu unlocked Grace's new phone and mentioned, in passing, that the store closed in twenty minutes. At home there was a family agreement taped to the fridge, with her father's handwriting on the amendment her mother had added: no devices at the dinner table, no exceptions for new phones.

Dalia pocketed her phone. "So sharing passwords on my steps. Bad idea, huh?"

Grace thought about all the afternoons on those steps, the good ones and that one. "Maybe," she said, and slid her new phone into her pocket, screen down.

activity: to explain how a bill becomes a law by passing through the legislature
knowledge_domain: to explain how a bill becomes a law by passing through the legislature
fact: Under the US Constitution, a bill becomes law without the president's signature if it is not returned within ten days, Sundays excepted, while Congress is still in session.
story:
The gym smelled like floor wax and coffee, and a line of people curled past the fold-out tables marked "Precinct 4." Austin followed his mom because Saturdays at the polling station beat Saturdays at home, and because he was still holding the little paper cylinder Ms. Sutton had given him. Inside it was a rolled strip of paper with tiny writing, like a scroll. On Friday she had said, "You each get one step of how a bill becomes a law. Monday, you articulate your step to the class, no reading off the card." Austin's card said the last step, and he was not at all sure he could say it out loud.

He remembered the moment Ms. Sutton handed it over, the way she tapped the paper and said the president was only part of the ending. He had assumed the ending was simple: Congress passes a bill, the president signs it, done. But his card didn't say that. His card said the president could do nothing and the bill could still become a law, which made no sense at all. Wasn't doing nothing the same as saying no? He turned the scroll over in his hands and looked for a clue.

"Are you in line, young man?" A poll worker with vigorous white eyebrows was grinning at him.

"Sort of. Can I ask you something? Do you know how laws get made?" Austin unrolled the card, his hands careful with the soft paper the way his mom was careful with her ears, folding the cartilage gently when she put in her earrings. "Congress votes yes, then the president has it. Then what if he just... never does anything?"

The worker rubbed his chin. "Then you get to the interesting part. If Congress is still in session and he doesn't return it within ten days, Sundays excepted, it becomes law without his signature. No pen, no stamp."

"Sundays don't count?" Austin said. He did the math on his fingers, skipping Sundays, and something clicked into place. Doing nothing wasn't the same as saying no, not while Congress was sitting there waiting. Silence could mean yes, but only on a hidden schedule.

"Where'd you learn to ask that?" the man asked.

"School. Monday I have to say it in front of everyone." Austin rolled the scroll back up, then found his mom in line. "Mom, quick. Congress passes a bill, the president does nothing for ten days, Sundays excepted, Congress still in session. What happens?"

His mom thought, failed, and laughed. Behind her, a woman in a red coat said, "Tell me too."

Austin cleared his throat. "Okay. But it starts with an idea, so you'll need the whole story."

activity: to read latitude and longitude on a map to give the location of a city
knowledge_domain: to read latitude and longitude on a map to give the location of a city
fact: By convention, a location's latitude is written first and its longitude second, as in about 40 degrees north, 74 degrees west for New York City.
story:
Theo held the map so close to his nose that Tomas laughed and said he looked like a raccoon inspecting a sandwich. They were sitting on a log by the campsite, and Mr. Oliveira had given them a challenge: find the exact spot of New York City using only numbers and a paper map, no phones allowed.

"Forty degrees north," Theo read off the card Mr. Oliveira had printed. "Seventy-four degrees west." He ran his finger along the horizontal lines first, then the vertical ones, and tapped a spot. "There. Easy."

Tomas squinted at the map. "That's in the ocean, isn't it?" It was. Their dot sat in blue water, a hundred miles from anywhere, unless fish had built a city.

"That can't be right," Theo said. He flipped the card over, shook it as if the answer might fall out, and stared at the map again. On the drive up, they had passed a hillside covered in giant white turbines, their blades turning slow and lazy, and the landscape around camp was sparse, mostly pine trees and bare rock. Somewhere in his brain, watching those blades go around and around, he had started thinking about how the map worked like a grid, like the net under a trampoline.

"Wait," he said. "Latitude comes first, then longitude. So I do the sideways number first, then the up-and-down one. Maybe I did it backwards." He tested it, dragging his finger along forty north, then down to seventy-four west, and the two lines crossed exactly on a little cluster of gray squares. "Look at that."

Tomas leaned in and grinned. "So New York City was in the ocean this whole time? The pigeons will be so surprised."

"I made a mirror mistake," Theo admitted. "Same numbers, flipped order. Different side of the world." He copied the right answer onto the card and marched it over to Mr. Oliveira, who was frying eggs over the fire.

Mr. Oliveira studied it and raised an eyebrow. "Spot on. By convention, latitude first, longitude second. Most people lose an hour to that mistake."

"Then most people should evaluate their life choices," Theo said, and Tomas threw a pinecone at him. Theo ducked, and the pinecone sailed past and landed with a plop in the dishwater bucket.

activity: building a project for the school science fair
knowledge_domain: building a project for the school science fair
fact: A baking soda volcano erupts because baking soda (sodium bicarbonate) reacts with vinegar (acetic acid) to produce carbon dioxide gas.
story:
Grace spread her materials across the library table: a plastic bottle, a box of baking soda, a jug of vinegar, and a notebook with three columns already ruled. Behind her, the tall windows let in the late afternoon light, and somewhere near the front desk a printer hummed. She had planned to build the classic volcano for the science fair, but Allan had laughed at her sketch yesterday and said every fourth grader in the building would have one too. That stung, mostly because he was right.

"Is that the volcano?" Jada asked, dropping into the chair across from her with a stack of books about Pompeii.

"It's not just a volcano," Grace said. "It's an investigation. Watch." She poured a careful half cup of vinegar into the bottle, added a spoonful of baking soda, and waited. Foam climbed the neck and slid down the sides, hissing softly. A few kids at the next table turned to look, and Ms. Mansour, the librarian, raised one eyebrow but said nothing, because Grace had laid down paper towels first, like she'd promised.

Grace wrote down what she saw. Then she rinsed the bottle, added a full cup of vinegar with the same spoonful of baking soda, and tried again. This time the foam shot higher, spattering the towels. Jada leaned in, chin on her hand. "So more vinegar makes a bigger eruption."

"That's what it looks like. But I want to know why it erupts at all." Grace flipped to a page she had found in a chemistry book the day before, one she'd had to postpone reading until her homework was done. She read the sentence twice, then pushed the book across the table so Jada could see it too. "It says a baking soda volcano erupts because baking soda reacts with vinegar to produce carbon dioxide gas." She tapped the last two words. "That's the whole secret. It's not magic, it's gas pushing everything up and out."

Jada read the page slowly. "So the gas is invisible. You never see it, you only see what it does."

"Exactly. Like the wind. You can't watch the cause, but you can watch the effect and measure it." Grace drew a small column in her notebook and labeled it height of foam. Then she frowned at her page. "I should have brought a ruler. I can't compare three trials if I just guess."

Allan appeared at the end of the aisle with a granola bar and a grin. "Ms. Mansour says you two are being negligent with the paper towels, by the way. Some dripped on the carpet."

"That was one drop," Grace said. "And it's vinegar, it dries clean." She held up the bottle. "Do you want to see something better than a plain volcano?"

He sat down. Grace lined up three cups on the table, side by side, and poured in different amounts of vinegar, smallest to largest, while Jada copied the numbers into the notebook. The room was quiet except for the scratch of pencils and the soft creak of a chair by the window.

"Same baking soda in each one," Grace said. "One spoonful, every time, so the only thing changing is the vinegar. Then we'll know the vinegar amount is what makes the difference." She held the spoon above the first cup and looked at the two of them. "Ready? Count with me."

activity: to track how a symbol changes meaning across the chapters of a novel
knowledge_domain: to track how a symbol changes meaning across the chapters of a novel
fact: In Harper Lee's To Kill a Mockingbird, published in 1960, Miss Maudie explains that it is a sin to kill a mockingbird because mockingbirds do nothing but sing their hearts out for us.
story:
Ethan slid To Kill a Mockingbird across the library table and flipped to page 90, where he had tucked a torn slip of paper. "I'm going to map it," he told Edouard. "Every time the bird shows up, I write the page, the chapter, and what it seems to mean right there. Then we watch the meaning move."

"That sounds like a lot of writing," Edouard said, but he pulled his chair closer anyway.

The first note was the big one. Ethan read it aloud: "'Remember it's a sin to kill a mockingbird.' That was Atticus. And Miss Maudie explains it, because mockingbirds don't do one thing but sing their hearts out for us." Edouard nodded slowly, and Ethan wrote: chapter 10, the bird equals something innocent that only gives.

"But then it jumps," Ethan said, hunting forward. "Chapter 21, after the trial. The mockingbird just appears in the dark and stops singing, right when the courtroom goes quiet." He copied the page number down. "Same bird, totally different feeling." He tried to condense three pages of scribbled notes into one column, crossing out words until only short phrases remained. That was when he noticed something. Characters kept lining up with the bird. He grabbed a fresh sheet and made a second list: Tom Robinson, who only helped. Boo Radley, who left gifts in the tree. "It's not about a bird at all," Ethan said. "The book keeps pointing at people."

"That's a huge idea," Edouard said. "What do you call that in English class? A symbol?"

Mr. Adeyemi passed by with an armload of returns and glanced at the two lists side by side. "You've made yourself a tracking chart, I see. Keep going, gentlemen." He set the books down and smiled. "Some of my best students started exactly like this, with paper covered in arrows."

Marilyn dropped into the seat across from them and peered at the page. "Why is 'Boo Radley' written next to a bird?" Ethan tapped his list. "Because the bird is basically an ambassador," he said. "It carries the meaning from character to character." Marilyn raised her eyebrows, so he pushed the novel toward her and pointed at chapter 10. "Read this part. Miss Maudie explains it. Mockingbirds don't do one thing but sing their hearts out for us, so killing one is a sin. Now watch who in this book only sings."

Marilyn read, then looked up. "Wait. Is Tom Robinson a mockingbird?"

"Write your name at the top of the next sheet," Ethan said, already turning to chapter 25.

activity: to settle a disagreement over a game by naming the problem and agreeing on a fair rule
knowledge_domain: to settle a disagreement over a game by naming the problem and agreeing on a fair rule
fact: In "divide and choose," one person splits something into two parts and the other picks first, so the divider has a reason to make the parts equal.
story:
The rain drumming on the gym roof meant no outdoor recess, so Nicolas and Beckham claimed the last good basketball before anyone else could grab it. Renee's class arrived two minutes later, and she walked straight over with her arms crossed. "We reserved this court yesterday," she said. Beckham hugged the ball tighter. "You didn't write it down," he said, "so it doesn't count." Nicolas could feel the afternoon starting to fracture, the way it always did when they argued about who got what.

"It's our ball, though," Beckham said. Nicolas was about to back him up when he remembered his cousin's birthday party last summer. The two of them had almost wrestled over the final slice of chocolate cake, which was clearly the most nutritious part of the meal as far as Nicolas was concerned. Then his cousin had said, "Let's do divide and choose." Nicolas had cut the slice into two pieces, and his cousin picked first. Somehow neither of them could complain afterward, and Nicolas had spent the walk home trying to figure out why it worked.

"Wait," he said now, bouncing the ball once. "Here's an idea. One team splits the court time into two parts. The other team picks which part they want first." Beckham frowned. "Who splits it?" "We do, since we had the ball first," Nicolas said. He was already thinking it through. If they made one part longer, Renee's class would just take that part and leave them the short one. The only split that couldn't be used against them was an even one.

Renee thought about it while her classmates generate... no, she thought about it while her classmates shuffled impatiently behind her. "Twenty minutes and twenty minutes," she said. "Both halves have to be exactly the same, or we pick the better one." "Deal," said Nicolas. Beckham still looked grumpy, but he let go of the ball long enough to shake on it.

Mr. Rossi, who monitored the gym on rainy days, watched them set the timer on his stopwatch and start the first half. At the switch, nobody argued, which felt strange in a good way. Renee even passed to Beckham once, right before she scored. As they lined up for the last shot of the half, she said, "Same thing next rainy day?" Nicolas spun the ball on his finger and grinned. "You split, we choose."

activity: hosting a grandparent who comes to stay for a week
knowledge_domain: hosting a grandparent who comes to stay for a week
fact: The body's sense of thirst weakens with age, so older people can become dehydrated without feeling thirsty.
story:
Grandpa Ray had been at Mason's house for four days, and so far the visit had been one long list of things he refused to admit. He refused to admit the recliner was comfortable, he refused to admit he liked Mason's dog, and on Saturday he refused, from his lawn chair in the backyard, to admit he wanted anything to drink.

"I'm not thirsty," Grandpa said, waving his hand like he was brushing away a fly. "Quit fussing."

Mason stood by the hose and frowned. Something wasn't adding up. Grandpa had eaten two salty pretzels, sat in the sun for an hour, and gotten up twice to stand in the shade looking dizzy. Mason had once read the back of a sports drink bottle at the community centre, and one line had stuck with him: thirst signals weaken as people age, so older folks can end up dehydrated without ever feeling it. At the time he'd thought it was tedious label trivia. Now it felt like a clue. The problem was invisible, so Mason decided to test it the only way he could, with a sneaky experiment.

He filled a pitcher at the kitchen tap, dumped in ice, sliced a lemon that was slightly too old, and carried it outside on a tray like a waiter in a movie. "It's not for you," he announced. "It's for me and Oakley. He's coming over. You can't have any."

Grandpa narrowed his eyes. "That's my glass."

"It's my glass, in my backyard, and my lemonade, which I made through a tedious process of squeezing." Mason set the tray on the picnic table with exaggerated care. "Enjoy not drinking it."

Grandpa drank three glasses in twenty minutes.

When Oakley arrived, he was mid-story about his little sister, who had tried to mediate a fight between two squirrels and gotten a cracker stolen for her trouble. He stopped, staring. "Did your grandpa drink that whole pitcher?"

"Every drop," Mason said, grinning. "Turns out if you tell him it's mine, it becomes his." Grandpa snorted so hard he nearly dropped the empty pitcher, and Mason got him a refill before he could pretend he didn't want one.

Later, while Oakley and Grandpa argued about whether a cloud looked like a whale or a very tired horse, Mason slid a water bottle onto the arm of the lawn chair without a word. Grandpa looked at it, then at him.

"You're getting sneaky," he said.

"You're getting predictable," said Mason, and Grandpa laughed so hard he sloshed water on his shoes.

activity: volunteering at a community food bank for the first time
knowledge_domain: volunteering at a community food bank for the first time
fact: A food bank is usually a warehouse that collects and stores large amounts of food, while a food pantry is the local place where people pick up food directly.
story:
The sign said "Community Food Bank" in tall blue letters, but the building behind it was the animal shelter where Tyler's neighbor, Mr. Tehrani, worked. Tyler pushed through the door with his permission slip crumpled in his pocket. Arnaud and Joanna were already stacking canned soup onto tall metal shelves, and dogs barked somewhere down a hallway on the other side of a thin wall.

An hour passed, and Tyler noticed something odd. Boxes kept arriving, and volunteers kept sorting and stacking, but not one person came in needing food. He nudged Joanna. "Where are all the customers?" She shrugged and kept counting pasta bags. Arnaud whispered that maybe nobody in town was hungry this week, which sounded wrong to Tyler. People didn't stop needing dinner on a Tuesday. He looked at the mounds of sorted food, more than a hundred families could eat in a month, and a thought began to take shape.

"I think this is the wrong kind of place for picking up," Tyler said slowly. "It's a warehouse. It collects and stores big amounts of food." He grabbed a folded map taped near the phone and traced the delivery routes marked in red. Every route ended somewhere else, at churches and schools. "The place where people actually pick up food is called a pantry," he said, tapping a dot three streets over. "There has to be one there today." Mr. Tehrani came out from the shelter side carrying a clipboard, and Tyler asked if they could load the van for the two o'clock run.

They rode over with buoyant spirits, and the parking lot at the little pantry was already lined with people carrying bags. Tyler handed crate after crate through the doorway, feeling like some kind of ambassador between the big quiet warehouse and this noisy, grateful line. Later, a mother let her daughter choose a box of cereal, and the girl hugged it like a puppy from Mr. Tehrani's kennels, the kind you nurture and take home. "See you Saturday?" the pantry manager called as they drove off. Tyler waved and said, "I'll be at the warehouse, where it all starts."

activity: noticing the changes of growing up and puberty
knowledge_domain: noticing the changes of growing up and puberty
fact: The prefrontal cortex, the part of the brain involved in planning and controlling impulses, keeps developing through the teenage years and into a person's twenties.
story:
The problem started before the car even moved. Violet had spent her camping savings on a glittery skateboard she did not need, and now her mom was driving her to Georges's house with the receipt burning a hole in her backpack like a guilty secret. She had planned to save for six more weeks. She had promised herself. Then she saw the board gleaming in the shop window, and her money had leaped out of her pocket before her brain could raise a hand and say, wait.

"Do you still have that science magazine?" she asked, because Georges was the kind of kid who kept every issue stacked under his bed like treasure. He did, and in the back seat he flipped through it while Kim leaned over his shoulder, smelling faintly of orange soda. "Here," Georges said, tapping a page. "This is about you." He wanted to be a brain surgeon someday, so any article about brains was big news to him, and he read aloud whenever anyone let him.

Violet took the magazine. The article said the prefrontal cortex, the part of the brain involved in planning and controlling impulses, keeps developing through the teenage years and into a person's twenties. She read it twice. "So I'm not broken," she said slowly. "I'm under construction." Kim snorted so hard the soda nearly came out her nose, which was not helpful but was funny.

"So it's a verdict," Kim said, holding out her hand for the magazine. "Your brain says not guilty yet." Violet wasn't sure that logic was credible, but it felt better than thinking she was just bad with money. She formed a plan on the spot, the way you do when a big idea transports you. She would leave her wallet at home on Saturdays. If the planning part of her brain was still being built, she would build scaffolding around it until the real thing caught up.

"We could test it," Georges said, bouncing a little on the seat. "All three of us. One month, no impulse buys. I'll chart it. Graphs, everything." Kim agreed only because she wanted to beat Georges at something, anything, and a chart was a battlefield like any other. The car pulled up outside Georges's house, and Violet dug into her backpack, pulled out the receipt, and held it up to the rearview mirror so her mom could see it in the glass. "Can we stop at the skate shop on the way home?" she asked. "I want to return it before my brain changes its mind."

activity: to shade a sphere with a light source to show highlight, shadow and cast shadow
knowledge_domain: to shade a sphere with a light source to show highlight, shadow and cast shadow
fact: Hatching shades an area with rows of parallel lines, and cross-hatching adds another set of lines crossing them to make the area darker.
story:
Lucas sat on the back steps with a pen and a blank page from his notebook. Ms. Zhao, the neighbour whose yard backed onto his, had offered to teach him to draw a sphere, but she had lent him only a pen. "A pencil gives you grey," she said over the fence. "A pen gives you lines. Make them work." The sun was behind him, so the old basketball on the grass had a bright spot on top, a dark curve along the bottom, and a long shape stretched across the grass beside it. That stretched shape was the part he wanted most.

His first attempt looked flat. He had pressed harder in places, but the pen made the same black no matter how hard he pushed. He tore the page out, crumpled it, and started again. The highlight was easy, he just left that circle white. The shadow under the ball needed to be somewhere between white and black, and he had no grey.

He tried drawing rows of short lines inside the sphere's edge, all going the same way, like rain falling sideways. The area became lighter than solid black but darker than the empty page. It worked. On the darkest curve near the bottom, one set of lines was still not enough, so he added a second set crossing the first, making little diamonds of white shrink between the crossings. That patch went darker than anywhere else. The stretched shape on the grass got the crossing lines too, since it lay under the ball and caught no light at all.

Holly leaned over the fence a few minutes later, holding her phone. "What's that called, the lines thing?" she asked. Lucas held the page up. "Rows of parallel lines is hatching," he said. "When you cross them with another set, it's cross-hatching." Holly typed it into the art app she used, which stored every technique in a database you could search by name. She was skeptical that a drawing done only in lines could look round, but she looked at the page for a while before she said anything.

"It does look round," she admitted. "The ball on the grass does too."

Lucas copied the drawing one more time to be sure he could do it again, and this time he angled the light source from the left, just to see what changed. The highlight moved, and the long shadow swung around toward Holly's fence. He pinned the page to the fence board facing Ms. Zhao's yard and got out his pen to try a cone.

activity: to give a two-minute speech with an opening hook, three points and a closing
knowledge_domain: to give a two-minute speech with an opening hook, three points and a closing
fact: People tend to remember the first and last items in a list best, a pattern called the serial position effect, which is why openings and closings matter.
story:
Penelope stood at the front of Room 12 with her note cards sweating in her hand. Her speech was about owls, which should have been thrilling, since owls are nocturnal hunters that can swivel their heads almost all the way around. Instead, she had opened with "Hello, my speech is about owls," which made Alix yawn so loudly that Ms. Wardak looked up from her desk.

After class, Alix caught her in the hall. "I only remember the head-swiveling part," Alix admitted. "And that you said 'thank you' at the end. What were your other points?"

"That's the problem," Penelope said. "I put my best fact, the silent flight, right in the middle. It got buried." She flipped through her cards and recounted the whole speech again, point by point, while Alix listened. Then Alix frowned.

"Wait. In Ms. Wardak's demo this morning, she listed five snacks, and I only remembered the chips at the start and the cookies at the end." Penelope grabbed Alix's sleeve. "Maxime! Come here. Tell her the snacks from the demo." Maxime, who was passing with his backpack half unzipped, said, "Chips, cookies, and, um, something about crackers? Maybe?" Penelope did a small hop. "It's the serial position effect," she announced. "People remember the first and last items in a list best. Ms. Wardak said the name under her breath, but I heard it."

"So your middle point is doomed," Maxime said solemnly, like a doctor delivering bad news.

"Unless it doesn't stay in the middle." That evening Penelope rebuilt the speech. Her new opening hook was a metaphor: an owl is a shadow with wings. Then silent flight went first, head-swiveling second, huge eyes third, and her closing looped back to the shadow. In class the next day she delivered it, and even Ms. Wardak put down her pen.

Alix raised her hand before the applause ended. "Silent flight. Shadow with wings. I remember everything."

"Everything?" said Maxime. "Even the middle?"

"Especially the middle," Alix said. "It was first."

activity: to fast, pray or keep a day of rest for part of a day as their family does and explain why
knowledge_domain: to fast, pray or keep a day of rest for part of a day as their family does and explain why
fact: During Ramadan, Muslims eat a meal called suhur before the dawn prayer, then go without food and drink until sunset.
story:
The community hall smelled like cardamom and burnt toast, which was odd, because Maya was supposed to be the one explaining Ramadan tonight, and the toast was technically her fault. She stood at a little table near the stage, holding a paper clock she had made, with a sunrise sticker on one side and a sunset sticker on the other. Behind her, Denis and Hana were setting out dates and cups of water for the evening meal, sneaking one date each when they thought nobody was looking.

"Okay," Maya said, "when the sun is right there, you stop. But here's the part everyone gets wrong." She flipped the clock over to show a dark side with a tiny drawing of a plate of eggs. "You wake up before dawn, in the dark, and you eat a meal called suhur before the dawn prayer. Then you go without food and drink until sunset." Denis frowned. "You wake up on purpose? Before the sun?" "My alarm went off at four," Maya confided, lowering her voice like she was sharing a secret code. "My dad shuffled into the kitchen in his robe looking like a sleepy penguin, and my little brother fell asleep with a piece of toast in his hand."

That morning came back to her as she talked: the kitchen dark except for the humming fridge light, the whole family gathered around the table eating eggs and drinking water slowly, carefully, like they were filling up a water bottle for a long hike. She had thought fasting would be mostly about being hungry, but the strange part was the quiet. No radio, no rushing, just spoons and yawning and her mom whispering, "Drink more, it's a long day."

The crowd in the hall was mostly neighbours, plus Ms. Fraser from down the street, who had brought a lemon cake "for after sunset, I hope." Maya demonstrated the fasting part by turning the paper clock from sunrise to sunset, then back again. "So you can eat when the sun goes down?" Denis asked, holding up a date. "Right at sunset," Maya said. "And honestly, after waiting all day, that date tastes like the best thing ever invented."

Then Hana, who had been studying the window, pointed at the clouds stacking up outside. "Precipitation coming," she announced in her best weather-reporter voice. "If it rains, no sunset stickers visible." Maya laughed and taped a flashlight to the back of the clock, just in case. The lights in the hall flickered once, abrupt as a blink, and somewhere in the kitchen the toaster pinged again. "Toast round two!" her dad called out, and Maya ran for it before her brother could fall asleep holding another slice.

activity: to describe their family and pets in a new language using full sentences
knowledge_domain: to describe their family and pets in a new language using full sentences
fact: In Spanish, the masculine plural "hermanos" can mean brothers, or brothers and sisters together, so "Tengo dos hermanos" might describe one brother and one sister.
story:
Sebastian raced into Spanish class holding his notebook like a trophy. Today Mr. Clarke had promised they would learn to describe their families in full sentences, and Sebastian had been practicing all week. "Tengo un perro," he whispered to himself as he slid into his seat. "Tengo un gato y un perro." He had even written a message to his pen pal, Marta, in Mexico City, telling her about his dog Biscuit and his little brother, and he was dying to read her reply.

Mr. Clarke handed out a stack of letters that had arrived that morning, and Sebastian tore his open so fast he nearly ripped the page in half. Marta wrote neat, careful Spanish. He understood most of it: she loved swimming, she had a cat named Luna, and then a line that stopped him cold. "Tengo dos hermanos." He frowned. Last month Marta had told him about her brother Luis and her sister Ana. Two hermanos? He read it three times. Maybe she had a new baby brother and Marta had just forgotten to mention it, but that seemed like big news to leave out.

He leaned over to Ellie's desk and showed her the line. "Marta has a brother named Luis and a sister named Ana," he said. "So why does she say dos hermanos?" Ellie squinted at the paper. "Maybe hermanos means siblings," she guessed. Sebastian drummed his pencil. There was a way to find out. Mr. Clarke had put family photos on the board from his own vacation, including one of his two sisters building a sandcastle, waves about to submerge their moat. Sebastian raised his hand. "Mr. Clarke, how would you say you have two sisters?" "Tengo dos hermanas," Mr. Clarke said, moving on to the next slide. Sisters, hermanas. Brothers, hermanos. But what about one of each?

Sebastian tried an experiment. He wrote on a scrap of paper, "Mi amiga Finnley tiene un hermano y una hermana. Finnley tiene dos hermanos. ¿Sí o no?" and passed it to Finnley two rows over. Finnley, who had grown up hearing Spanish from her grandmother, read it and scribbled back fast. "Sí! In Spanish, hermanos can mean brothers, or brothers and sisters together." Sebastian read the note twice, then waved it in the air like a winning ticket. That was the answer. Marta hadn't forgotten anything, and there was no mystery baby. One word was doing two jobs, and once you knew the formula, whole sentences clicked into place.

At the end of class Sebastian wrote his reply to Marta in full sentences, feeling almost sophisticated. "Tengo un hermano y una perra. Tengo dos..." He paused, grinned, and finished anyway. "Tengo dos mascotas." He sealed the envelope and dropped it in the mailbox on Mr. Clarke's desk. "Two hermanos and two mascotas," he told Ellie on the way out. "This language is full of secrets, and I'm finding all of them."

activity: cooking or baking a meal for the family
knowledge_domain: cooking or baking a meal for the family
fact: Caramelization is browning that happens when sugar alone is heated, which makes it a different reaction from the Maillard reaction, which also needs amino acids.
story:
Oliver stood in the baking aisle of Frisch's Grocery with a crumpled list in his hand, staring at a bag of sugar and thinking about the roast. Last Sunday he had sprinkled sugar over sliced pears and slid them under the broiler, and they had turned a deep glossy brown, almost the same color as the crust on his dad's roast beef. Tonight his parents were both working late, and he had promised a proper dinner for once, roast and all, plus a caramel sauce for the ice cream. He wanted to know if the two browns were actually the same thing, because if they were, maybe he could get the same result either way.

"Are you going to buy that sugar or marry it?" said Zayd, who had tagged along to carry the basket and steal samples from the deli counter.

"I'm thinking," Oliver said. "The pears browned with just sugar. But the roast browns too, and there's no sugar on it at all. So it can't be the same browning."

"Maybe the oven just makes everything brown," Zayd said, plucking a free toothpick of sausage from the sample tray and waving it like a tiny ambassador of the deli department, as he put it, sent to recruit hungry ten-year-olds.

Oliver tested that idea. Plenty of things in the oven did not brown the same way, and he remembered the plain bread he had baked that stayed pale no matter how long he left it. He put the sugar in the basket. "I think sugar alone browns when you heat it," he said. "The roast has to be something else, because the meat has no sugar."

At home, Zayd's older brother texted them one word and a link, and the word made Oliver laugh out loud: the meat browning was called the Maillard reaction, which also needed amino acids, things meat had and sugar did not. "So it's a different reaction from mine," Oliver said, pouring sugar into the pan. "Mine's caramelization. Sugar alone, plus heat. That's it." He decided he could eliminate half his worry right there; the sauce did not need the meat's trick, only its own.

The sugar melted, went amber, then copper, smelling like toasted marshmallows, and he whisked in cream so fast it hissed like an angry cat. The roast came out mahogany. Zayd leaned over both dishes, sniffing.

"Same color," Zayd said.

"Not the same," Oliver said, spooning warm caramel over the ice cream and feeling pretty immune to further argument. "Different reaction."

Zayd took a bite, closed his eyes, and said, "Different and better."

activity: words such as anxiety, stress, coping and boundaries used to talk about mental health
knowledge_domain: words such as anxiety, stress, coping and boundaries used to talk about mental health
fact: During the fight-or-flight response, the adrenal glands release adrenaline, which makes the heart beat faster and breathing speed up.
story:
The poster on the wall behind Mr. Aydın's desk showed a beach at sunset, and Ivy counted the palm trees while she waited, because counting things helped. There were seven. Her heart was hammering anyway, the same way it had hammered this morning before she gave her book report, and she was tired of it.

"Your teacher said you froze up there for a minute," Mr. Aydın said. He slid the tissue box closer to her side of the desk, though she hadn't cried.

"I didn't freeze. My heart just started pounding like I was running from something, but nothing was happening. Nobody was chasing me." She paused. "Morgan says it's anxiety. Ophelia says it's stress. They can't both be right."

"Maybe they're both partly right." He turned his monitor toward her. On the screen was a simple diagram, and he pointed at two small shapes sitting on top of the kidneys. "These are the adrenal glands. When the body decides something is an emergency, they release adrenaline, and that makes your heart beat faster and your breathing speed up."

Ivy leaned in. "So my body thought a book report was an emergency?"

"That's one way to put it."

She sat back and thought about it. If the pounding was just adrenaline, then it wasn't proof that something terrible was about to happen. It was a false alarm, and alarms could be tested. "Can I try something?" she asked. "Ophelia has to give her history presentation next period. If this is a pattern, her heart should pound too, even though there's no danger. Can I go watch?"

Mr. Aydın smiled and wrote her a pass. "That's your own coping strategy. I like it."

In the hallway Ivy found Ophelia by the water fountain, hands pressed flat against her cheeks. "Feel my pulse," Ophelia said. "It's like a drum solo." Ivy pressed two fingers to her friend's wrist and felt the racing beat, fast and frightened, with nothing anywhere in sight to fear.

"Your adrenal glands are just being dramatic," Ivy said. "Next time it happens, breathe slow and let the alarm ring itself out." She rolled her shoulders back. "Come on. Let's go survive your presentation together."

activity: the idea that prices rise when many people want something scarce and fall when it is plentiful
knowledge_domain: the idea that prices rise when many people want something scarce and fall when it is plentiful
fact: In the Dutch Republic, prices for rare tulip bulbs soared in the winter of 1636 to 1637 and then collapsed in February 1637, when buyers stopped showing up.
story:
Victor pushed his peas around his plate while his dad ladled out more soup. The kitchen smelled like garlic and onions, and Victor's mind was somewhere else entirely: on the shoebox under his bed holding eleven Sharktooth trading cards, including the silver-fanged one that Nika had offered three sandwiches and a broken telescope to get.

"I still don't get it," his dad said. "Last month those cards were everywhere. Now?"

"Now nobody wants them." Victor took a bite of bread. "Everyone wants Dragonfyre cards instead."

His little sister banged her spoon and chanted, "Dragonfyre, Dragonfyre," with the contagious excitement of a person who had no idea what a trading card was.

Victor remembered the day he'd traded his skateboard for the silver-fanged Sharktooth. Edward had held the skateboard with both hands, like it was made of glass, and said, "This card is only going to go up. My cousin says there are like a hundred of these in the whole school." Victor had felt smart then, like he'd beaten everyone to something. Now he wondered whether Edward's cousin had simply made that number up.

At school it had been just the same, but bigger. Mr. Wright, who taught social studies and collected old coins, had listened to Victor argue about card prices one afternoon and told him about something that happened long ago. "In the Dutch Republic," Mr. Wright had said, leaning back in his chair, "prices for rare tulip bulbs soared in the winter of 1636 to 1637, and then collapsed in February 1637, when buyers stopped showing up." Victor had laughed out loud. Tulips. Grown-ups had done the exact same ridiculous thing with flowers.

He tested the idea the next day at lunch. He set the silver-fanged card on the table in front of Nika and said, "Two sandwiches." Nika slid it back with one finger. "One sandwich. Half a sandwich." Edward, across the table, wouldn't even look up from his Dragonfyre folder. The card hadn't changed. It was still silver, still sharp-toothed, still rare. The only thing that had changed was that everyone wanted something else now, and there were boxes of Sharktooth cards at the store where there used to be none.

Victor sipped his soup and watched steam curl off his dad's bowl. He thought about the boy in the Dutch Republic, four hundred years ago, who must have traded a whole cart or a cow for one bulb, feeling exactly as smart as Victor had felt. Maybe he'd even had a friend like Nika who stopped showing up.

"Are you okay?" his dad asked. "You look like you lost a war."

"I lost a skateboard," Victor said.

His sister banged her spoon again and shouted, "Half a sandwich!"

activity: to explain why ancient Egyptians built the pyramids and how the Nile shaped their farming
knowledge_domain: to explain why ancient Egyptians built the pyramids and how the Nile shaped their farming
fact: Each year the Nile flooded Egypt in late summer, fed by heavy summer rains in the highlands of Ethiopia far to the south.
story:
Evelyn sat on the low stone wall of the war memorial with her notebook balanced on her knees. Her report on ancient Egypt was due first thing tomorrow, and one question had stopped her cold: why did the Nile flood every single year in late summer, when Egypt was a desert where almost no rain ever fell? Ilyes plopped down beside her, and Brady leaned against the wall, squinting at the carved names of soldiers.

"Give up and just write that it rained a lot," Brady said.

"Then I'd be wrong," Evelyn said. She flipped through her research pages. "Look at this weather record. Cairo got almost nothing all year. The probability of a flood caused by local rain is basically zero. So the water came from somewhere else." She traced the river on the map with her finger, all the way to the bottom edge of the page. "The Nile goes south. Far south."

Ilyes leaned over. "It says here the river runs down from the highlands of Ethiopia."

Evelyn sat up straight, her attention suddenly acute. "That's it. The flood happens in late summer, which is when the summer rains are hammering Ethiopia, way down there. All that water has to go somewhere, and the river is the chute. Egypt gets a flood with no clouds." She grabbed her water bottle and tipped a slow trickle onto the sloped stone beside the names, watching it gather speed downhill. "See? Pour it at the top, it arrives at the bottom."

"That's the Nile in miniature," Ilyes said.

Mr. Rao, who had been straightening wreaths by the flagpole, walked over before she could spill more. "We don't intervene between visitors and the memorial stone, please," he said gently. Then he glanced at her map and smiled. "Ethiopia. My grandfather farmed along that river his whole life."

"You mean the flooding actually helped?" Evelyn asked.

"His whole village waited for it," Mr. Rao said, and moved on.

Evelyn wrote fast, pen scratching. The flood was the point, not the problem. It left wet black mud on the fields, mud a farmer could plant straight into, which explained why the pharaohs could feed thousands of workers to stack stone into pyramids for decades. Brady read over her shoulder and gave a low whistle.

"Tomorrow, you start with the bottle trick," he said.

Evelyn screwed the cap back on, tucked the map under her arm, and ran for home to finish the last page.

activity: the idea of a hypothesis as a testable guess that an experiment can support or overturn
knowledge_domain: the idea of a hypothesis as a testable guess that an experiment can support or overturn
fact: Repeating an experiment several times helps show whether a result is real or just happened by chance.
story:
Bodie propped the ramp against the fence, dropped his red car, and it rolled down and crossed the chalk line half a length ahead of Oliver's blue one. Bodie threw both arms up. "Fastest car in the backyard. Forever."

"It won one race," Oliver said.

"One race is enough. If you want proof, I'll even quantify it. My car won by six inches. Write it down."

Oliver wrote it on the back of a seed packet: red, six inches. Then he said, "Let's race again."

The second time, the blue car won by two inches. Bodie said the grass was uneven. They moved the ramp to the patio. Third race: blue won again. Fourth race: red won, barely. By the fifth, Bodie had stopped doing his victory arms and was crouched at the bottom of the ramp, chin on the concrete, watching the wheels.

"Something's off," he said. "One car can't be fastest sometimes and slowest other times."

Oliver looked at the seed packet, at the scribbled list of results. Red, blue, blue, red, red, blue. It looked random, like coin flips. He had a guess about why, a testable one: maybe the cars weren't different at all, and the winner was decided by small stuff, where exactly they were released, tiny bumps in the concrete. "Here's my hypothesis," he said. "Neither car is faster. Any race could go either way."

"That's a boring hypothesis," said Bodie.

"It's still a hypothesis," said Ms. Halvorsen, leaning over the fence with a watering can. "Means a guess you can test."

"Then I'll test it," Oliver said. He put the same car in the same spot and held it with the same finger, and did that ten times in a row while Bodie marked wins and losses on the seed packet. The red car won four, the blue car won six, close to half and half, which fit his guess. Then Bodie insisted on one more round, lost it, and announced he was selling the red car.

"You'd get fifty cents for it," Oliver said.

"It's a collector's item."

"It has a wheel held on with tape."

Christina came through the gate with her bike helmet still on, saw the ramp, and asked to enter a car. She didn't have one, so she raced Oliver's blue car against itself, borrowing a green one from her backpack, and the green one won twice in a row.

"That proves green is fastest," Christina said.

Oliver held up the seed packet, which now had thirty-one tally marks. "It doesn't prove anything yet. Race it ten more times and see if it's consistent."

Christina raced it eleven more times, because Bodie said extra ones should count double, and the green car won five and lost six.

"Coin flip," Bodie said, lying flat on the patio with the tape-wheeled car held up against the sky. "My whole career was a coin flip."

"My dad says that about his mortgage," Christina said, and pedaled home.

activity: to follow a recipe to bake muffins from start to finish including preheating the oven
knowledge_domain: to follow a recipe to bake muffins from start to finish including preheating the oven
fact: Preheating means waiting until the oven has reached the set temperature before the batter goes in, so baking starts at the right heat.
story:
Jeremy had promised to bring muffins to the class bake sale, and this morning was his only chance to make them. He spread the recipe on the counter, scrutinizing each line as if a single missed word might ruin everything. Miley sat on the stool beside him, cracking her knuckles. "My mom says you're competent if you can bake without calling for help," she said. "No pressure."

He measured the flour, the sugar, the oil, and the eggs, and folded in blueberries until the batter looked like the picture. The last step before filling the tray was the one that bugged him. Preheat oven to 400 degrees. He stared at the oven dial. The oven would take ages to warm up, and the bus came at 8:40. So he made a decision: he filled the muffin cups, slid the tray inside, and turned the oven on right then, timer and all.

When the timer beeped, the muffins were pale and squat, nothing like domed bakery muffins. Miley leaned over them. "They look like something a rodent would bury for winter," she said. Jeremy laughed, but his stomach sank. He had followed every line of the recipe except that one word, preheat. Maybe that was the whole problem. He checked the oven manual, and there it was: preheating means waiting until the oven has reached the set temperature before the batter goes in, so baking starts at the right heat. His first batch had started in a cold oven that crept upward, and the muffins had never gotten the right heat at the start.

He turned the dial to 400 and watched the orange light glow. Miley tapped her watch. "We can still catch a later bus." When the light blinked off and the little thermometer said the oven was ready, Jeremy mixed a fresh batch, filled the cups, and slid the tray into real, full heat. Twenty minutes later the tops were golden and rounded. He lifted one out, still steaming, and held it up. "Now that," Jeremy said, "is a muffin."

activity: getting a first pair of glasses
knowledge_domain: getting a first pair of glasses
fact: Herman Snellen developed his eye chart of rows of shrinking letters in 1862.
story:
Tyler was missing the ball again. Ryan threw it, and it smacked the fence behind him before Tyler's glove even moved. That made three in a row.

"Are you ignoring me on purpose?" Ryan called across the playground. "You're notorious for that in math class."

"I'm not ignoring you," Tyler said. "I'm not doing it on purpose." He tried to work out what was going wrong. When the ball left Ryan's hand, it looked sharp. Halfway across, it went fuzzy, like a smudge on a window. Ryan's face was fine up close, and even the letters on his hoodie from across the fence were clear. The problem seemed to be the middle distance, and that felt like a pattern worth testing. He asked Ryan to toss the ball slowly and watched carefully. Close, clear. Middle, blurry. Far, a pale streak. It wasn't Ryan, and it wasn't the ball. Something about his own eyes.

He mentioned it to the school nurse that afternoon, and she sat him in front of a chart on the wall, rows of letters shrinking downward. Tyler squinted at the second row and got it wrong. "The big E is E," he said, "and after that it's basically soup."

The nurse slid a lens into a frame and held it up. The letters snapped into focus so neatly that Tyler laughed out loud. She wrote a note for his parents: he needed glasses, his first pair.

"Who invented this chart, anyway?" Tyler asked, peering at it.

"A doctor named Herman Snellen," she said. "He made this design in 1862."

"That's older than anyone's great-grandparents," Tyler said.

"It is," the nurse agreed, smiling.

The next week Tyler wore his new glasses onto the playground. Ms. Silva-Jayasuriya, who supervised recess and would only permit catch in the open area away from the swings, watched him catch Ryan's first throw cleanly, then the second, then a hard one that stung his palm.

"Better?" Ryan shouted.

"Better," Tyler called back, and fired the ball home.

activity: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
knowledge_domain: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
fact: Sikh gurdwaras serve langar, a free communal meal offered to every visitor regardless of religion, often with everyone seated together on the floor.
story:
Nora pressed her palm flat over the ball of dough and rolled outward, slow and even, until it spread into a circle the size of a small plate. In the kitchen at home, steam fogged the window above the stove, and her mother turned the griddle with a hiss. Tomorrow was the celebration at the gurdwara, and their job tonight was forty rotis for the meal called langar.

The doorbell rang twice, fast, the way Linden always rang it. He came in still wearing his soccer cleats and stood at the counter with his hands in his pockets. "My mom wants to know how much it costs," he said. "The ticket for the dinner."

"There isn't a ticket," Nora said.

"Everything costs something. Festivals, dinners, all of it."

Nora rolled another circle and thought about that. She had watched people stream through the langar hall her whole life, Sikhs and non-Sikhs, neighbours and strangers, and she had never once seen anyone pay. If Linden didn't believe her, arguing would cease to help after a minute or two. What he needed was to see it himself.

"Come with us," she said. "Then you'll know. At the gurdwara, langar is a free meal for every single visitor, no matter what religion they are, and everyone sits together on the floor to eat it. My dad says that's the whole point of it."

Linden picked up a ball of dough and squashed it, so Nora showed him how to roll from the middle out. His first roti came out shaped like Australia, and his second one like a cloud, and by the fifth he had something close to a circle. "So it's a legitimate free meal," he said. "Not a trick, not a sample."

"A real meal," Nora said. "And if you come early, you can help serve the rotis like I do. That's the best part."

He stacked his cloud-shaped one carefully on top of the others, as if it were too precious to lose. "Can I bring this one? I want to hand it to somebody myself."

The griddle hissed, the steam valve on the pot rattled softly, and Nora slid the last perfect circle off the heat. "Grab the flour tin," she said. "We still have twenty to go."

activity: getting a first pair of glasses
knowledge_domain: getting a first pair of glasses
fact: In nearsightedness, light from distant objects focuses in front of the retina instead of on it, most often because the eyeball is slightly too long.
story:
Nolan had memorized the first three rows of the science review from his phone on the bus, but the quiz was going to be written on the board, and from the back row the board was a gray smear. He had blamed the teacher's handwriting, then the glare, then his seat. Now Ms. Ma had pulled him out of third period and walked him down the hall to the nurse's office, because the vision screening van was leaving the school at noon and it was already 11:40.

"Read the bottom line for me," the nurse said, pointing at a chart across the room. Nolan squinted. The letters swam. Then she held up a card six inches from his face, and he read every word on it without effort.

"That's weird," he said. "Close stuff is fine. Far stuff isn't. It's like the board is broken and my phone isn't."

"It's not the board," the nurse said, and turned to get a folder. While her back was turned, Nolan looked at the diagram taped inside the cabinet door, the one she'd left open. It showed an eye as a circle with a curved lens in front and a thin layer along the back labeled retina. Light from a distant object came through the lens and crossed to a point marked with an X. The X floated in the middle of the eye, in front of the retina, not on it.

Nolan stared at the diagram, and an idea began to build. If the crossing point fell short of the back of the eye, then the eye itself must be too deep somehow. He raised his hand. "Is it that the eyeball is, like, a little too long? So the focus lands in front of where it's supposed to?"

The nurse paused, and something in her face that was impossible to read, some small private approval she could not convey with words, crossed it anyway. "That's the most common reason," she said. "It's called nearsightedness." She pulled a trial frame from a drawer and slid a lens into it. "The lens moves the focus back onto the retina."

"Wait," Nolan said. "Can I test something first?" He curled his fingers into a fist and left a tiny gap, a pinhole, and looked through it at the chart. The bottom line snapped into focus: E, Z, O, P. He grinned so wide his cheeks hurt. "It works. It actually works."

"That's the oldest trick in the book," the nurse said, laughing, and handed him the trial frame. He put it on and the whole room jumped out at him, sharp and layered, the clock hands and the door handle and the pen marks on Ms. Ma's clipboard. He had spent a month thinking he was bad at science, maybe bad at school, and none of that had been true. Nobody was immune to being wrong about themselves, he thought, not even him.

"The van leaves in ten minutes," Ms. Ma said, checking the clock. "And your quiz is at one o'clock."

"Then I'll take the quiz wearing these," Nolan said, "and I'll read every word on that board." He kept the trial glasses on and walked out into the bright hallway, still blinking at the sharp edges of everything.

activity: to draw a food chain from the sun to a top predator and explain what happens when one link disappears
knowledge_domain: to draw a food chain from the sun to a top predator and explain what happens when one link disappears
fact: Robert Paine introduced the term 'keystone species' in 1969 for a species whose removal changes its whole community far more than its numbers would suggest.
story:
Mr. Cardinal set a bucket of colored pencils on the lab bench and told the class to illustrate a food chain that ran from the sun all the way to a top predator. Christopher stared at his blank page. His first drawing had looked sparse, just four lonely arrows, so he had crumpled it up. Now he started over: sun, then grass, then grasshoppers, then frogs, then a heron at the top with its long neck curved like a question mark.

Alyvia leaned over from the next stool. "The tricky part is question two," she said. "What happens if one link disappears? I wrote that everything shifts down one level, but I'm not sure."

"My dad says that's the dilemma with fish," said Maisy, chewing her pencil. "Take one thing out and you don't know what breaks until it breaks."

Christopher remembered the science museum trip. He and Maisy had built a stone arch from wedge-shaped blocks while a docent watched, and when Maisy pulled out the single middle top stone, the whole arch had clattered onto the table. Later, in the car, Maisy's dad had told them that a scientist named Robert Paine had introduced the term "keystone species" in 1969, for a species whose removal changes its whole community far more than its numbers would suggest. Christopher had thought that was just a cool fact about arches. Now he tapped his pencil against the lab bench and wondered if a food chain could have a keystone too.

He tested a simple idea. With his eraser he wiped the frogs off his page, then redrew the arrows as if frogs had vanished. Grasshoppers, with nothing eating them, got fat arrows multiplying across the paper. Grass thinned out. The heron at the top lost its meal. One erased link, and the entire page looked wrong. He tried removing a grasshopper next and redrew it; that changed things too, but not nearly as much. The same number of creatures removed, a completely different amount of damage.

"Mr. Cardinal," Christopher said, holding up both pages, "can one middle link be like the middle stone in an arch?" Mr. Cardinal smiled and said that was a fine comparison, and that Christopher should show the class. At the front of the room, Christopher drew the food chain on the board, erased the frogs, and watched Alyvia's eyes go wide.

"That's it," she said. "That's what happened to my page too, I just couldn't see it until you erased yours."

"So the frog is the stone in the middle," said Maisy. "Pull it out and the whole thing comes down."

Christopher capped his pencil and drew one final arrow, straight from the sun to the heron, then laughed and erased it. "No," he said. "It has to go through everything."

activity: to follow a recipe to bake muffins from start to finish including preheating the oven
knowledge_domain: to follow a recipe to bake muffins from start to finish including preheating the oven
fact: A toothpick pushed into the centre of a muffin that comes out clean or with a few dry crumbs shows the muffin is baked through.
story:
The restaurant kitchen smelled like cinnamon and butter, and Luke tied his apron so tight it almost cut him in half. Ms. Popal had agreed to let him bake a batch of muffins from start to finish, as long as he followed the recipe himself. "The whole formula," she said, tapping the card. "Every step, in order." Luke read it twice. The first line said to preheat the oven, so he turned the dial and listened to the oven rumble awake while he measured flour and cracked eggs. His friend Arabella leaned against the counter, narrating like a sports announcer. "He stirs. He spills a little. He wipes it up with dignity."

"The oven's hot, the batter's in the pan, the timer is set," Luke said. "That's the whole game."

"Except the part where we wait," Arabella said.

They washed dishes while they waited, and Ms. Popal warned them away from the spray bottle by the sink. "That stuff is toxic, so keep it far from anything you're going to eat," she said, moving it to a high shelf.

When the timer beeped, Luke pulled the pan out with the big padded gloves. The muffin tops looked pale, not golden like the ones in the bakery window. "Maybe they need more time," Arabella said. "Or maybe they're done and just look pale." Luke frowned. The outsides gave no answer, because the important part was hidden inside.

Then he remembered the box of toothpicks by the coffee station. He pushed one straight into the centre of the middle muffin and pulled it out. Wet batter clung to it. "Not done," he announced. Back into the oven they went. Five minutes later the tops were golden, and a fresh toothpick came out clean, with only a few dry crumbs. He tested one more, just to be sure, and it came out clean too.

Ms. Popal broke a muffin in half and steam curled out of it. Luke had thought baking was mostly luck, but now he saw it was more like a test you could actually check.

"See?" Arabella said. "Told you waiting was part of the game." She bit into a muffin and gave a thumbs up.

activity: the idea that posts, photos and location data can be stored, shared and seen by strangers
knowledge_domain: the idea that posts, photos and location data can be stored, shared and seen by strangers
fact: iPhones and Android phones let you choose, app by app, whether an app may use your location always, only while you are using it, or never.
story:
Landon's cursor hovered over the email from the game company. "Congratulations! Your Galaxy Raiders stats have been reviewed by our partner advertisers." He hadn't told anyone his address. He hadn't told anyone anything except his username, SkullPilot7.

He thought back to Saturday, when Nancy had leaned over his shoulder at the kitchen table, watching him play. She wanted to beat his high score before Monday so she could be the first in their grade to reach Sector Five, and she'd been practicing every night. "You should enter the tournament," she'd said, jabbing a finger at the glowing banner. "Free entry. They just ask for your phone stuff." Landon had tapped Agree without reading a word. It had seemed like a small thing, like swatting a fly.

Now the email said his "local achievements" had earned him a coupon for the pizza place two blocks from his house. The exact pizza place. The one he could see from his bedroom window. Landon sat very still, and the house sounded different than usual, the refrigerator humming like something listening.

He picked up his phone and opened Settings, scrolling down to the long list of apps. There it was, Galaxy Raiders, and next to it a word that made his stomach drop: Always. He tapped it, and a screen appeared with three choices. "Always, Only While Using the App, or Never," he read out loud, slowly. Every app had the same three choices, sitting there the whole time like switches on a wall he'd never noticed. He checked his other apps one by one. His homework app said Never. His weather app said Only While Using. Galaxy Raiders glowed with its Always like a parasite that had moved in while he wasn't looking.

He tried to remember when it had changed. Had it always been that way? He thought about evading it, deleting the app and pretending the whole thing was nothing. But Nancy was practicing for the tournament with the same game, and if it was watching him, it was watching her too. He switched Galaxy Raiders to Only While Using the App and typed a message to her: "Check your settings. Location. Look what yours says."

Her reply came back three minutes later, in her usual assertive style, all capitals: "ALWAYS?? HOW LONG HAS IT SAID THAT?" Then, before he could answer: "CHANGED IT. NEVER. DONE."

Landon deleted the email, emptied the trash, and opened the tournament page one last time. At the bottom, in small gray letters, it said entries required location access for eligibility. He closed the tab. On Monday, he'd tell Nancy they could race to Sector Five the old-fashioned way, side by side on the couch. Downstairs, his dad called that pizza was ready, and Landon took the stairs two at a time.

activity: to explain why ancient Egyptians built the pyramids and how the Nile shaped their farming
knowledge_domain: to explain why ancient Egyptians built the pyramids and how the Nile shaped their farming
fact: Egyptians used nilometers, stairs or pillars marked with measurements beside the river, to track how high the Nile flood rose and predict the size of the harvest.
story:
Colton pressed his nose against the glass case in the Egypt room of the history museum and groaned. His worksheet had one question left, the one worth the most points: explain why the pyramids mattered to the Nile farmers, and how the river shaped their whole year. He had already written that the pyramids were tombs, because that much was obvious, but the rest of the page stared back at him, blank.

"You're radiating panic," said Lauriane, appearing beside him with her clipboard. "You can actually feel it from three feet away."

"It's worth twenty points," Colton said. "Ms. Greco said the answer is somewhere in this room, and I can't find it."

Maximilian pointed across the room. "Then try over there. That's the only exhibit we haven't looked at, and you're the systematic one. You've checked everything else."

Colton followed him to a stone staircase built into the floor, roped off with a velvet cord. The steps went down into a shallow pool of blue-green water, and carved into the stone wall beside them were lines, one above another, like a giant ruler. His first instinct was that it was a well, but a well wouldn't need marks on the side. He crouched and counted the lines. Eleven of them, evenly spaced, rising out of the water toward the top step.

The words on the small brass plate came into view as he leaned closer. "Nilometer," Maximilian read aloud. "That's what it's called. A nilometer."

Colton's brain caught fire. The lines, the water, the stairs beside the river. "Wait," he said slowly. "The Nile floods every year, right? That's in the video we watched. So they could watch the water climb the steps, past the carved lines, and they'd know exactly how high the flood rose." He turned to Lauriane. "And if they knew how high the flood was, they'd know how much water the fields got. Which means they could predict the harvest before a single seed went in the ground."

Lauriane was already flipping through her notes. "That's it. That's the whole chain. Flood, then harvest size, then how much food everyone has." She grabbed her pencil.

Colton knelt at the velvet rope and dipped his finger toward the water, just to see where today's line would be, and a museum guard cleared his throat from across the room.

"Okay, okay," Colton said, standing up, grinning. "Twenty points, here we come."

activity: to add and subtract fractions with unlike denominators by finding a common denominator
knowledge_domain: to add and subtract fractions with unlike denominators by finding a common denominator
fact: To subtract fractions with unlike denominators, rewrite both with a common denominator first: three quarters minus one third becomes nine twelfths minus four twelfths, which is five twelfths.
story:
The tutoring centre smelled of dry-erase markers, and Mr. Tesfaye's rule was that nobody left until their worksheet was done. Dominic had eleven of twelve problems finished. The twelfth sat there like a dare: three quarters minus one third.

Melodie dumped her craft bag on the table across from him. "Channing's birthday is Saturday," she said. "I need ribbon for the gift. I've got three quarters of a metre left on the roll, and the bow takes a third of a metre. Do I have enough?"

"That's my problem," Dominic said, turning his worksheet toward her. "Exactly that. Which is suspicious."

He stared at the two fractions. They didn't match, so subtracting them felt like trying to dock a boat with the rudder on land. Then he had an idea. He wrote down all the twelfths: one twelfth, two twelfths, all the way up. He circled the ones that lined up with a quarter and with a third.

"Both of them can be twelfths," he said. He tested it on the whiteboard. Three quarters became nine twelfths. One third became four twelfths. He subtracted the four from the nine and got five twelfths.

"Is five twelfths of a metre enough for a bow?" he asked.

Melodie held up her thumb and forefinger, squinted, and did math of her own with her hands. "Barely. I'll make the bow smaller and accommodate the rest of the ribbon by wrapping it twice."

"Affluent people just buy more ribbon," said Channing, sliding into the seat beside her with a smoothie from the shop in the affluent part of town, the one with the marble counter.

"Affluent people don't tutor here on Thursdays," Melodie said.

Mr. Tesfaye walked past, glanced at the whiteboard, and put a small check mark next to problem twelve without a word. Dominic wrote five twelfths on his worksheet, capped his marker, and slid it across the table to Melodie. "For your bow," he said. "Receipt not included."

activity: customs such as greetings, gift-giving and table manners that differ between cultures and households
knowledge_domain: customs such as greetings, gift-giving and table manners that differ between cultures and households
fact: In Japanese homes, shoes are taken off in an entrance area called the genkan before stepping inside.
story:
Ruby rang her aunt's doorbell with her elbow because her arms were full of gift bags, and behind her Safiya balanced a tray of cookies. The party started in forty minutes, and Mom had put Ruby in charge of the front hallway. "Eliminate the clutter," Mom had said on the drive over. "First impressions happen at the door."

The door swung open, and Ruby nearly stepped inside. Then she froze. A neat row of shoes sat along one wall, sandals and sneakers lined up like passengers waiting for a train, and beyond them a stack of soft slippers sat on the wooden edge. Two floor levels, almost. Safiya leaned close and whispered, "It's like a shoe checkpoint."

"You take your shoes off in the genkan before you go in," said Jamie, Ruby's cousin, appearing from the kitchen with a stack of napkins. "That's what Uncle calls the entrance. Come on, you have to see the table." Ruby stepped down, pulled off her sneakers, and set them in the row, toes facing the door like everybody else's. A pair of blue slippers waited for her, exactly her size, which felt like a secret invitation. She slipped them on and followed Jamie, Safiya hopping on one foot behind her.

The dining table was already a miniature ecosystem of dishes, each cousin claiming a bowl of chopsticks, a plate, a folded napkin. Aunt showed Ruby how to pass the rice with both hands, and when Ruby gave Safiya's mom a gift bag, the woman pressed it back once, twice, before accepting it with both palms, which made Safiya giggle. "You have to offer it twice," Jamie whispered. "It's a whole system." Ruby decided to test it and offered the cookies to Uncle the same way, holding them out, drawing them back, holding them out again. He laughed and took them with both hands, bowing his head.

Later, Mom asked Ruby to move the paper lanterns away from the candles on the sideboard. "They're flammable," Mom said, and Ruby scooped them up, padding across the floor in her blue slippers. At the door, the row of shoes had grown to fill the whole wall, the last pair tipped sideways, still warm.

activity: to walk to the corner store alone, buy milk and count the change
knowledge_domain: to walk to the corner store alone, buy milk and count the change
fact: Many stores stock shelves 'first in, first out', putting older products at the front, so the carton with the latest date is often at the back.
story:
Alexia held the ten-dollar bill so tightly it wrinkled. Her mother had said it three times at the door: milk, the blue carton, and come straight home. The grocery store was only two blocks away, but Alexia had never walked there alone, and the crossing guard at Maple Street watched her wait for the light with what felt like extra attention.

Inside, the store hummed with the quiet commerce of a Tuesday evening. A man stacked oranges. The cashier waved at someone she knew. Alexia found the dairy case at the back and reached for the first blue carton, then stopped. Her mother had once grabbed a carton from behind the front row and said, "They push the old ones forward." Alexia turned the front carton over. The date stamped on it was sooner than the one on the carton behind it, and the one behind that was later still. She checked three more, just to be sure the pattern held, then took the carton with the latest date from the back. It felt like a small, private victory over whoever arranged the shelves.

At the register the cashier said, "Four twenty-nine." Alexia handed over the ten and counted the change in her palm while the cashier watched: five dollars, then seventy-one cents. "Five seventy-one," Alexia said, and the cashier nodded. She counted it again on the way to the door, because a plausible answer was not the same as a certain one.

Outside, Azalea from her class was leaning against the bike rack. "You went in alone?" Azalea asked. "My mom still won't let me." Alexia had assumed Azalea, who was louder and faster at everything, had been running errands for years. She felt her opinion of Azalea shift, and something like shyness in Azalea too, which she had never noticed before. "It's not that bad," Alexia said. "Want to walk back with me? I'll show you the milk thing."

"What milk thing?"

"The dates. The newest cartons are at the back." The streetlight came on as they started home, and its glow refracted through the plastic window of the milk carton, throwing a wobbling stripe of light onto the sidewalk. Azalea stepped on the stripe, missed, and stepped again. "Tomorrow," she said, "I'm asking my mom."

"Do it in the morning," Alexia said. "She'll say yes before coffee."

activity: to read contour lines on a topographic map to find the steepest slope of a hill
knowledge_domain: to read contour lines on a topographic map to find the steepest slope of a hill
