fact: The U.S. Geological Survey's standard 7.5-minute topographic maps use a scale of 1:24,000, so one inch on the map equals 2,000 feet on the ground.
story:
Mr. Rahimi spread a wrinkled topographic map across the science room table and clipped its corners down. "There's a prize for the team that correctly identifies the steepest side of Miller Hill," he said. "You have until Friday."

Austin leaned over the map with Liya and Rayden. Brown squiggly lines looped everywhere, nested inside each other like puddles after rain. Rayden wanted to just guess the west side because it "looked rugged." Liya rolled her eyes at that. "That's your bias talking," she said. "You always pick west." Austin said nothing. He scrutinized the lines near the summit, where they crowded so tightly they almost touched. Somewhere in the back of his mind, his grandfather's voice complained about a hike that looked short on paper and took all day.

That night he found a note taped inside his backpack, in his grandfather's blocky handwriting. "Found my old USGS map of Miller Hill from 1971. Check the scale in the corner before you argue with anyone. And eat something green." Austin dug out a magnifying glass and read the tiny print at the bottom edge of the classroom map. It said the scale was 1:24,000. He remembered the ruler in his pencil case.

The next morning he got to school early and laid the ruler across the map. Where the contour lines bunched tightest, on the east flank of the hill, he measured the whole steep stretch: it was half an inch. He did the math twice, because the first answer seemed too easy. One inch on the map equals 2,000 feet on the ground, so half an inch meant 1,000 feet of real hillside, crossed by five tightly packed contour lines. On the west side, where Rayden's rugged look lived, the lines spread wide and lazy, and the same ruler showed two full inches, which was 4,000 feet of gentle walking. The steep side and the flat side covered the same height change, but one packed it into a quarter of the distance.

"East," Austin announced at lunch, pushing the map toward his friends. "The east slope. The lines are squished together there." Rayden frowned. "But the west looks steeper. All those jagged edges." Liya tapped the corner of the map. "Those jagged edges are cliffs drawn as symbols, not slopes. Look where the lines actually stack up. It's like the whole east face is symmetrical, one loop inside another, tighter and tighter, like a target."

On Friday Mr. Rahimi checked each team's answer against his marked copy. When he reached their table, he raised an eyebrow at Austin's ruler, still lying across the east slope. "Correct," he said, and dropped three granola bars on the map. Austin took the one closest to the steep side.

activity: to read contour lines on a topographic map to find the steepest slope of a hill
knowledge_domain: to read contour lines on a topographic map to find the steepest slope of a hill
fact: Contour lines spaced evenly apart show a slope that has the same steepness all the way along it.
story:
Theodore spread the topographic map across the kitchen table and weighted the corners with a mug, a stapler, and his mom's artisan bread, which she'd left cooling on the rack and which now smelled too good to ignore. He tore off a chunk anyway. Tomorrow was the first big snow, and April and Cayson were counting on him to pick the sledding hill, because last year Cayson had chosen a slope that looked gentle at the top and turned into a wall of terror halfway down. Cayson had flown off a jump he never agreed to and landed in a briar patch. This year they would choose with science.

Mr. Rao, who kept maps the way other neighbours kept garden gnomes, had lent him one of the hill behind the school. The brown squiggles covering it were contour lines, and Theodore had figured out that each line was the same height as the next, so lines crammed together meant the ground rose fast. He ran his finger along the west side, where the lines bunched up like startled caterpillars. Steep, then steeper, then whoa. That was the briar patch side. He exhaled slowly, as if the map itself might calm down.

Then he noticed something odd about the northeast slope. The lines there sat an even distance apart, the whole way from bottom to top, like rungs of a ladder. He grabbed a ruler and measured between them at the top, the middle, and the bottom. All the same. His pencil tapped the table. Even spacing, even spacing. If bunched lines meant steep, then lines spaced evenly apart had to mean the slope kept the same steepness all the way along it. He tested the idea against the west side, where the gaps shrank and grew and shrank again, and there it was: the deadly sudden steepening, hiding in plain sight.

He texted a photo to April: "Northeast slope. Lines are even the whole way, so it stays the same steepness the whole way. No surprise cliffs. Tell Cayson to keep his hands inside the sled."

Her reply came in seconds: "You measured a hill with a ruler and a loaf of bread. You're a nerd and a genius."

"A genius," Theodore texted back, and tucked the map into his backpack, one corner still smelling faintly of sourdough.

activity: to mediate an argument between two friends without taking a side
knowledge_domain: to mediate an argument between two friends without taking a side
fact: In mediation, each person usually gets to tell their side without being interrupted while the other person listens.
story:
Harper stood in Ms. Nkosi's backyard with a paper plate of cake she couldn't eat yet, because Jorge and Mckayla were both talking at her at the same time, and neither of them would stop. It was Jorge's birthday party, which made it worse. The piñata hung from the maple tree, swinging a little in the breeze, and thirteen kids were waiting to hit it, but Jorge and Mckayla had planted themselves by the fence and refused to move until somebody settled things.

"You promised the first turn to me," Jorge said, "and then you told everyone it was Mckayla."

"I never said first," Mckayla said. "I said I had a turn coming. That's different."

"You said it right there, in the garage, I heard you."

"Okay, hold on." Harper held up both hands like a crossing guard. She had watched her aunt resolve a dispute between two neighbors once, and the thing she remembered most was that it didn't start with deciding anything. "Here's what we'll do. Jorge, you tell your side, and Mckayla, you just listen until he's done. Then you get your turn, all the way through, no cutting in. Then I'll say what I think."

"That's like court," Jorge said, brightening. "Where the defendant gets to speak before anything happens."

"Except nobody here is on trial," Harper said. "You both just get a turn."

Jorge went first. He said he'd been handing out blindfolds in the garage, and he'd told Mckayla she'd get a turn, and he never said first. Mckayla opened her mouth twice, and twice Harper said, "Wait for your turn," until Mckayla folded her arms and waited. When it was her turn, she said the words "your turn" had sounded like "first turn" with the music so loud, and she'd honestly believed it.

Harper thought about that. Both stories could be true, which made both of them credible in a way, and the real trouble wasn't a lie, it was a loud garage. She pointed at the piñata. "Jorge, since it's your party, you go first. Mckayla goes second and gets the good blindfold. And next time, go outside to make deals, before the music invades everything."

Mckayla grinned and grabbed the rope. "Deal. Now hand me that blindfold."

activity: to learn a traditional dance or song well enough to perform it at a community gathering
knowledge_domain: to learn a traditional dance or song well enough to perform it at a community gathering
fact: A Bharatanatyam dancer's first full solo performance is called an arangetram, meaning ascending the stage, and marks the end of their first formal training.
story:
The cemetery gate squeaked behind William, and he set his phone on the flat top of his grandmother's headstone, facing the little patch of grass where he always practiced. Her arangetram photo was buried somewhere at home in a shoebox, and he had stared at it all week: nineteen years old, gold-bordered sari, arms bent like temple carvings. Tomorrow was the community gathering at the temple hall, and he would perform the same alarippu she had performed, in front of everyone.

"It's called an arangetram," Aksel had told him on the bus, because Aksel's sister took the same classes. "It means ascending the stage." Omer had leaned over the seat. "So after you do it, you're done? Like graduating?" William had said maybe, and that word had followed him ever since. Done. He kept testing the idea against the photo, against the headstone, against everything, and it never quite fit.

He started the music and danced. Eight counts, then the abrupt shift his teacher always warned about, then the turn. On the turn his heel slid on the dew-wet grass, the same way it had at every practice that week. He stopped, breathing hard. He'd blamed his shoes, then the school gym floor, then nerves. But here the ground was soft everywhere, and he still slipped only on the turn. So it wasn't the floor. It was him. He hummed the counts alone, without the music, and found it: he was rushing the beat before the turn, arriving early, weight already orbiting off his standing leg. The conductor inside his own chest had been dragging the tempo. He started again, slower, planted his heel, and the turn came around clean as a wheel.

He wiped the grass off his palms and looked at the headstone. Done after tomorrow? He didn't believe that anymore; the turn had taught him there was always a next thing to find. He pressed play on his phone and took his opening stance beside her name.

activity: to add and subtract fractions with unlike denominators by finding a common denominator
knowledge_domain: to add and subtract fractions with unlike denominators by finding a common denominator
fact: Estimating first catches mistakes: one half plus one third must be more than one half but less than one whole.
story:
Grandpa's kitchen smelled like butter and scorched optimism. He was in the garage hunting for his old measuring cups, and Connor had exactly forty minutes before Aunt Rosa arrived expecting her birthday pie, which meant doubling the recipe on the faded card before the oven finished preheating.

The card was Grandpa's mother's, and Grandpa had inherited it along with a chronic inability to write recipes in normal amounts. Half a cup of cream here, a third of a cup of honey there, and every single number had to be doubled. "Eight halves," Connor muttered, scribbling. "And six thirds." He added them and wrote down fourteen ninths of a cup, because half plus third had turned into some strange business with a nine, and nine was bigger than eight, so it felt close enough.

He stared at the bowl. Fourteen ninths was nearly a cup and a half of cream going into a pie that should have been only a bit richer than the original. Something about that was wrong in a way he couldn't see, like a smell of gas with no flame lit. So he tested it the only way he could: in his head, with easy numbers. Half the pie was gone, then a third more. That had to land somewhere past the half mark but short of a whole pie, because half plus a third wasn't enough to finish it. His answer, though, had jumped right over one whole. More than a whole meant the estimate and the answer disagreed, and one of them was lying.

He called Amina, who answered on the second ring because she was avoiding her own homework. "How do you add halves and thirds?"

"Twelfths," she said, as if he'd asked the time. "Both of them turn into twelfths. Six twelfths plus four twelfths. Ten twelfths."

Connor hung up and checked. Ten twelfths was more than a half, less than one whole, exactly where the estimate said it should sit. His nine, wherever it had come from, was a stranger who needed to leave. He poured five sixths of a cup of cream, cut the lattice strips with the same careful symmetry his great-grandmother's photo showed on the card's back, and slid the pie into the oven with nine minutes to spare.

Flashback, brief: last Tuesday, Ms. Sharma had walked past his desk, tapped his paper where he'd written that one half plus one third equaled two fifths, and said only, "Try guessing first, then check yourself." At the time he'd thought it was a strange thing to say about math, which was supposed to be exact. Now he suspected she'd handed him a smoke detector.

The timer ticked. Aunt Rosa's car crunched into the driveway, and Grandpa came in from the garage holding a measuring cup he no longer needed. He looked at the oven, then at Connor's flour-dusted forearms, and raised an eyebrow.

"Ten twelfths," Connor said. "Don't ask."

activity: getting a first phone and learning to use it responsibly
knowledge_domain: getting a first phone and learning to use it responsibly
fact: The phone Martin Cooper used for the first handheld cell phone call weighed about 1.1 kilograms (2.5 pounds).
story:
Logan set the shoebox on the kitchen table and peeled back the tape, because his grandfather had wrapped the phone in an actual shoebox instead of a gift bag. Inside lay a slim black rectangle, lighter than Logan expected, and beside it a note in his grandfather's looping handwriting: "Handle with care. Talk to your mother about the rules." His grandfather was already pulling out a chair, the smell of coffee rising from his mug, while Logan's mother set down the family agreement she had typed up the night before. It restricted his screen time to one hour on school nights, and Logan had read it twice at breakfast hoping it would shrink.

"Two and a half pounds," Grandpa said, hefting the new phone in one palm and laughing. Logan took it back protectively, and that made his grandfather laugh harder. "You could have knocked someone out with the first one. Martin Cooper made the first handheld cell phone call, and that thing weighed about 1.1 kilograms, over two pounds of battery and case." Logan turned the fact over in his head while his mother slid the agreement toward him and set a pen on top.

"Half an hour," Logan said. "School nights, thirty minutes, and I get to keep the phone in my room if my grades stay up." His mother raised an eyebrow. He had a plan for testing her real reason, the hidden rule underneath the rule. He suspected she wasn't worried about minutes at all but about what he might do late at night, so he offered the one thing that mattered to her. "I'll hand it to you at nine, every night, no reminders. That proves I can handle the rest."

The phone buzzed before anyone answered. Khaleesi had already texted, because Jessa had told her the phone was coming today, and Logan's reputation as the last kid in class without one had apparently ended the moment the box left the store. "Is it true?" the message read. Logan typed back a photo of the phone on the kitchen table next to Grandpa's coffee mug, then sent a second one of the empty shoebox, which had sparked a small and controversial debate in the group chat about whether it was a hamster box or a rat box.

His mother signed her half, then watched him place the phone on the counter by the stairs, the spot he had chosen himself. Grandpa winked and drained his coffee. "Nine o'clock," Logan said, tapping the counter twice.

activity: to describe their family and pets in a new language using full sentences
knowledge_domain: to describe their family and pets in a new language using full sentences
fact: Spanish nouns have grammatical gender, so a male dog is "el perro" and a female dog is "la perra."
story:
The screen door banged behind Clara as she followed her grandmother into the kitchen, where a pot of cinnamon-scented coffee sat steaming on the stove. Amos trailed after them, hugging his notebook. He had a Spanish speaking contest on Friday, and he wanted every sentence to sound credible, which was why he had begged to come along. "Your grandmother's from Lima," he whispered. "If I can describe my family in front of her, the judge won't scare me."

"Start with pets," Clara said, spreading her flashcards on the table, cards she had made for Rosa, the speckled dog she had left sleeping on her own bed at home. "It's easier." Amos cleared his throat and recited, "Tengo un hermano y una hermana. Tengo un gato." Her grandmother nodded, tapping the table in a slow rhythm, and Amos grinned so wide Clara thought his face might split.

Then it was Clara's turn. Her hands felt cold even in the warm kitchen. She laid down Rosa's photo and said, carefully, "Tengo un perro. El perro se llama Rosa." Something flickered across her grandmother's face, a small tilt of the head, and then the old woman said one quiet word: "¿Perra?" Clara stared at the photo. She thought back to every card, every drill. The male dog on the worksheet had been "el perro," and the female one, she suddenly remembered, had been printed differently. "La perra," Clara said slowly, testing it like a step on thin ice. Her grandmother smiled and answered in careful English, "Yes. El perro is a male dog. La perra is a female dog." Clara looked at Rosa's speckled face, at the belly she had rubbed a hundred times without ever once thinking about the word for her.

"So I've been calling her a boy all week," Clara said, and laughed until she had to hold the table. Amos was already scribbling, muttering "el gato, la gata" under his breath, and on Friday, when he took the stage, he described his mother, his sister, and his female cat with his chin up. From the back row, Clara raised Rosa's photo where only she could see it. "La perra," she mouthed. "Ella se llama Rosa."

activity: breaking an arm and wearing a cast
knowledge_domain: breaking an arm and wearing a cast
fact: A greenstick fracture is a break where the bone cracks on one side and bends on the other, like a young green branch; it happens mostly in children because their bones are more flexible.
story:
Theodore sat on the crinkly paper of the exam table, holding his arm the way you hold a full cup of juice, careful and close. Annalise had dared him to ride his bike down the Thompsons' gravel path with no hands, and he had budgeted exactly three seconds of no-handed glory before the front wheel wobbled, the world flipped, and the gravel came up to meet him. Now his left arm throbbed under a bag of crushed ice, and Ms. Schneider, who lived next door to the Thompsons and had driven him here, was filling out forms at the desk outside.

The doctor came in with an X-ray film and clipped it to the light box on the wall. "Good news and strange news," she said. "Your arm is broken, but only partly."

"Partly?" Theodore stared at the pale bones glowing on the film. "How can it be partly broken? It's either broken or it isn't." That was how broken things worked. His old headphones were either working or dead. There was no partly.

The doctor tapped the film with one finger. "It's called a greenstick fracture," she said, and then she got called away to check on another patient, which was annoying, because now Theodore had a phrase and no meaning.

Annalise arrived ten minutes later, out of breath, carrying his backpack. "Is it broken? Tell me everything. Did you see your actual bone? Abbas thinks if you see your own bone you get to leave class early forever."

"It's broken but only on one side," Theodore said slowly, still looking at the X-ray. "The other side just bent." He said it out loud to hear whether it made sense, and to his surprise, it almost did. He tried to picture it. Outside the window, a wedge of migratory geese crossed the sky in a wobbly V, and he thought about the maple branches in his yard. In spring, when the branches were young and green, you could bend one and it would fold and crack on the outside of the bend while the inside just curved. He had done it a hundred times. In winter, the old dry brown branches snapped clean through, both sides, no bending at all.

"Wait," he said. "My arm is a green branch."

"What?"

"Greenstick. Like a young branch. Cracks on one side, bends on the other." He pointed at the film, tracing the thin dark line that stopped halfway across the bone, where the other side simply curved. "That's why it's mostly kids who get these. Our bones are more flexible. Grown-up bones are dry sticks. They snap."

The doctor came back in time to hear the last part. "Exactly right," she said, sounding pleased. She turned to Annalise. "He did my job for me."

They wrapped his arm in bright blue fiberglass, and Annalise wrote GO GREEN BRANCH on it before the doctor had even finished. Abbas arrived with a marker and added a drawing of a goose. It was still broken, and it still hurt, but as Theodore flexed his fingers out of the end of the cast, all five of them wiggling, he decided that partly broken was a variable he could live with.

"Three seconds of no hands," Annalise said, shaking her head as they walked out. "Was it worth it?"

Theodore looked down at his blue arm, crowded with writing and one crooked goose. "Ask me in six weeks."

fact: Snoring happens when relaxed tissues in the throat vibrate as air passes through them during sleep.
story:
Violet stood in the doorway of Eshal's bedroom with her sleeping bag under one arm and a problem in her head. She had never been to a sleepover before, and tonight she wanted it to go perfectly, which was hard when Eshal was already yawning at eight o'clock.

"You always fall asleep first," Ryan said, unrolling her own bag near the closet. "And then the noise starts."

"It's not that bad," Eshal said.

"It's a roar. Last time I couldn't hear my music over it."

Eshal flopped backwards on the bed, wounded. Violet chewed her lip. She hated the idea of Eshal feeling embarrassed, but she also remembered the science assembly where a guest had held up a model of a throat. "Snoring happens when relaxed tissues in the throat vibrate as air passes through them during sleep," the guest had said. Violet had thought it was boring then. Now it felt like a clue.

If the noise came from Eshal's throat, it had to come out of her mouth and nose and spread through the room like ripples in a pool. It wouldn't be equally loud everywhere. Violet tested the idea in her head: the farther from the source, the quieter the sound.

"Ms. Ba gives us ten minutes before lights out," she said, checking the clock. "Here's what we do. Ryan, you and I put our bags on the far side of the room. Eshal, you stay near the door. That's all. Nobody has to change anything about themselves."

Eshal sat up. "You're arranging the whole room around my snoring?"

"I'm arranging it around physics," Violet said, and Eshal laughed for real.

They dragged the bags across the carpet, compressing Ryan's into the corner to make room. At midnight, after a vigorous pillow fight that woke Eshal's mother, the snoring began, deep and rumbling, but from the far side of the room it sounded like a distant train.

"You were right," Ryan whispered through the dark.

Violet pulled her blanket to her chin and whispered back, "Science never sleeps. Well, except Eshal."

fact: Antiperspirants reduce sweating by temporarily plugging sweat ducts, while deodorants do not stop sweat but reduce or cover the smell.
story:
Colton stood in the middle of his bedroom holding his T-shirt away from his chest like it had betrayed him. The shirt was soaked through at the armpits, and it wasn't even hot in the room. He had noticed this happening for two weeks now, at school, at basketball practice, even sitting still during math. Last Tuesday, Tayla had scooted her desk an inch away from his, and when he asked why, she'd only wrinkled her nose. He'd spent the whole period pretending to read.

He remembered the shopping trip with his dad on Saturday, standing in the store aisle between two shelves. He had picked up one stick labeled deodorant and another labeled antiperspirant, and read the small print twice. The antiperspirant box said it reduced sweating by temporarily plugging sweat ducts. The deodorant box said nothing about sweat at all; it only said it reduced or covered odor. So the two things were not the same product at all. He had grabbed the antiperspirant, and now it sat on his dresser like evidence.

He tested it like a science experiment, because that was how his mind worked. Day one, no stick: by lunch his shirt was damp and Tayla was scooting again. Day two, the antiperspirant: his shirt stayed dry through a whole basketball practice, though afterward there was still a faint smell. So sweat and smell were two separate problems. Interesting. Day three, he used the antiperspirant and swiped his dad's deodorant over it too, then sniffed his shirt at noon and found nothing. Dry and fresh.

On Thursday, Camilla came over to work on their history project about kings and queens. She looked at the two sticks lined up on his dresser beside his authentic replica jersey, the one signed by his favourite player. "Why do you have both?" she asked.

"Antiperspirant stops the sweat," Colton said. "Deodorant doesn't stop it, it just covers the smell."

"That's actually smart," Camilla said. "My brother only uses deodorant and his shirts are soaked all summer."

Colton grinned. "It took three days of testing."

"Tayla will accuse you of trying to show off," she warned.

"Let her," he said, pulling on his jersey. "This room isn't a monarchy. I get to rule my own armpits."
